paragraphs: Belief propagation estimates probabilities in graphical models by passing messages between variables. It gives correct answers when the graph is a tree, but loops can make its answers inaccurate or prevent convergence. The paper addresses this gap by combining two approaches that account for interactions ordinary belief propagation can miss.

One approach uses cavity distributions to represent dependencies between messages. The other groups variables into small regions and models their interactions together, accounting for loops contained within those regions. Generalized Loop Correction brings these ideas into a single approach, drawing on both dependencies between messages and interactions within groups of variables.

The authors explain how their method relates to both existing families and evaluate its accuracy empirically. Their results suggest that it works effectively across the settings considered and can be substantially more accurate than either correction scheme. The contribution is a way to combine complementary sources of correction; the reported accuracy gains are empirical rather than a guarantee of exact inference on every graph.
icml-2012-a-generalized-loop-correction-.tldr: Generalized Loop Correction combines two approaches to correcting belief propagation and can substantially improve inference accuracy.

paragraphs: A contractive auto-encoder learns more than a compact representation of an input: it captures directions in which nearby inputs can vary while remaining plausible. The paper uses this local geometric information to construct a sampling procedure, turning the learned representation into a source of generated examples.

The key information comes from the Jacobian, which describes how the representation changes when the input changes. Its leading singular vectors identify local directions of variation, while the associated singular values indicate how much variation is plausible. The proposed stochastic process generates samples consistent with this structure and defines a distribution from which samples can be drawn.

In experiments, the process appears to converge quickly and move effectively between modes compared with Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Deep Belief Networks. The same intuition also guides training a second layer that pools features and becomes insensitive to local variations found by the first layer. The authors show that this can improve the representation of invariances and reduce classification error.
icml-2012-a-generative-process-for-contr.tldr: The paper uses local structure learned by a contractive auto-encoder to generate samples and learn representations that can improve classification.

paragraphs: Learning a model of a system is useful for control only if that model supports good decisions. Existing guarantees discussed in this paper assume that the learner's candidate models include the real system. The authors instead study the agnostic setting, where every available model may be an imperfect description of reality.

They propose an iterative method that connects model learning to no-regret online learning. Their result allows any no-regret online learning algorithm to serve in this approach and obtain a near-optimal policy, provided that some candidate model has low training error and a good exploration distribution is available. These conditions remain central even though exact representation of the real system is no longer required.

The approach covers both discrete and continuous domains. A demonstration on a challenging helicopter control problem provides evidence of its effectiveness and scalability. The broader contribution is a conditional route from imperfect system models to strong control performance, explaining how useful guarantees can survive when the model class does not contain the truth.
icml-2012-agnostic-system-identification.tldr: An iterative learning method offers near-optimal control guarantees with imperfect model classes, given low training error and good exploration.

paragraphs: Modified policy iteration is a dynamic programming framework that includes both policy iteration and value iteration. Its approximate versions matter when state or action spaces are too large, or infinite, for exact computation. This paper develops that approximate setting and examines how errors made during learning affect the resulting policy.

The authors introduce three algorithms extending fitted-value iteration, fitted-Q iteration, and classification-based policy iteration. They give a shared error propagation analysis that brings approximate policy iteration and approximate value iteration into the same framework. They also analyze the classification-based implementation with a finite amount of data, providing a treatment broader than the analyses of the other proposed implementations.

A central observation concerns the parameter in modified policy iteration. It controls the balance between errors in approximating values and errors in estimating the greedy policy, which chooses actions using those values. This makes the parameter relevant to final policy performance: it changes how the two kinds of approximation error contribute, rather than merely selecting between familiar algorithm names.
icml-2012-approximate-modified-policy-it.tldr: Three approximate modified policy iteration algorithms share an analysis showing how a parameter balances value approximation and policy estimation errors.

paragraphs: The paper applies Bayesian statistical learning to recovering hidden information in spread-spectrum watermarking systems. Its attack model takes a watermarked signal and jointly estimates both the watermark signal and the embedded sequence of message bits. The method does not require access to the watermark decoder.

Joint inference treats the unknown watermark and message as parts of one estimation problem. The authors develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler that updates model parameters through their conjugate full conditional posterior distributions. They also provide a variational Bayesian alternative, which further speeds convergence of the inference algorithm.

Experiments on synthetic signals and real images show recovery of a large portion of the embedded message together with a highly accurate estimate of the watermark signal. These results demonstrate that the observed watermarked signal can reveal substantial information under the proposed model, even without decoder access. The stated outcome is substantial recovery in the experiments, rather than a claim that every embedded message is recovered completely.
icml-2012-bayesian-watermark-attacks-b65.tldr: A Bayesian attack jointly estimates a spread-spectrum watermark and much of its embedded message without access to the decoder.

paragraphs: When observations from different data sources occur together, clustering can seek groups characterized by relationships across those sources. This paper develops a copula mixture model for that task. Its aim is to make dependency-seeking clustering flexible enough to accommodate different continuous distributions for the individual measured variables.

The approach extends mixtures of Canonical Correlation Analysis using copulas, which provide a way to describe dependence separately from marginal distributions. This separation allows arbitrary continuous marginal densities within the proposed multivariate model. The authors formulate it as a nonparametric Bayesian mixture and provide efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo inference for learning from the paired observations.

Experiments with synthetic and real data show significant improvements in clustering and in the interpretability of the results. The finding links the model's added distributional flexibility to useful empirical gains: allowing individual variables to have different distribution shapes can help expose relationships between sources. The stated scope concerns continuous marginals and co-occurring observations, which are central to the proposed formulation.
icml-2012-copula-mixture-model-for-depen.tldr: A Bayesian copula mixture extends dependency-seeking clustering to arbitrary continuous marginals, improving clustering and interpretability in experiments.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs whose components interact, so learning often requires searching a large space of possible combinations. Expressive interactions can make this inference step, and consequently exact learning, computationally intractable. Decomposed Learning addresses this bottleneck by limiting the part of the output space examined during training.

The important question is when such a restricted search preserves the result of exact learning. The authors give characterizations involving the problem's structure, the target parameters, and the correct training labels. Under the stated theoretical conditions, Decomposed Learning with limited inference is equivalent to exact learning, despite searching only part of the output space.

The paper also evaluates settings where those conditions may hold only approximately. There, its algorithms are significantly more efficient while achieving accuracies close to exact learning. This separates two contributions: a conditional equivalence guarantee and empirical evidence of practical usefulness beyond exact satisfaction of the assumptions. Together, they explain why reducing inference during training can retain much of the value of structured learning.
icml-2012-efficient-decomposed-learning-.tldr: Decomposed Learning restricts training-time inference, matching exact learning under stated conditions and approaching its accuracy efficiently in experiments.

paragraphs: Structured prediction with hidden variables must account for both relationships among outputs and information that is not directly observed. The paper presents a common framework for this setting. Hidden conditional random fields and latent structural support vector machines both appear as special cases, connecting two established approaches within one formulation.

To make the general formulation computationally manageable, the authors construct an approximation using duality and a local approximation to entropy. They then derive an efficient message passing algorithm with a convergence guarantee. The guarantee concerns the derived algorithm; the method still uses an approximation to the general structured prediction formulation.

The authors demonstrate the approach on image segmentation and on understanding three-dimensional indoor scenes from single images. In these tasks, they report better performance than hidden conditional random fields and latent structural support vector machines. The results support the usefulness of the unified formulation and its inference procedure for these visual prediction problems, while the convergence result gives a separate theoretical property of the algorithm.
icml-2012-efficient-structured-predictio.tldr: A unified framework for structured prediction with hidden variables yields a convergent message passing algorithm and improved results on two visual tasks.

paragraphs: Some matrix estimation problems call for two kinds of simplicity at once: many entries should be zero, and the matrix should have low rank. The paper targets this combined structure. Motivating examples include social and protein interaction networks whose adjacency matrices have a block-diagonal form in an appropriate basis.

The authors introduce a convex penalty that combines the ℓ1 norm with the trace norm. These terms encourage sparsity and low rank within the same estimation procedure. An oracle inequality describes how their effects interact depending on the target matrix, giving a theoretical account of why the two forms of structure should be considered together.

The paper also bounds generalization error for link prediction and develops proximal descent strategies to solve the optimization problem efficiently. Evaluations use both synthetic and real datasets. The contribution therefore spans a combined estimator, analysis of its statistical behavior, and practical optimization methods. Its focus is on estimating matrices that are sparse and low rank simultaneously, with the target's structure shaping the interaction between those goals.
icml-2012-estimation-of-simultaneously-s.tldr: A convex matrix estimator combines sparsity and low-rank penalties, with theoretical error analysis and efficient proximal optimization.

paragraphs: Plant traits help researchers understand and predict how ecosystems adapt to environmental changes. The TRY database gathers these measurements globally, but extensive missing data limits analyses that require several traits together. This paper treats the gaps as a matrix completion problem while incorporating the hierarchical relationships among plants.

Traditional matrix factorization methods can estimate missing entries from patterns in observed values, but the methods discussed here do not use the plant kingdom's phylogenetic hierarchy. Hierarchical probabilistic matrix factorization adds that information to trait prediction. The approach therefore uses both patterns in the measurements and the biological hierarchy associated with the plants.

Experiments demonstrate high prediction accuracy, show that incorporating the hierarchy is effective, and indicate that the model captures correlations among traits. These findings support using phylogenetic structure as useful information for filling missing measurements. The contribution connects a general prediction technique to a defining property of the ecological data, making the hierarchy part of the model used to estimate the unobserved traits.
icml-2012-gap-filling-in-the-plant-kingd.tldr: Hierarchical probabilistic matrix factorization uses plant phylogeny to predict missing traits accurately and capture trait correlations in experiments.

paragraphs: Two-sample tests ask whether datasets come from the same distribution, while independence tests ask whether variables are related. This paper connects two families of statistics used for these tasks: energy distances and distance covariances, and distances between distribution representations in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.

The equivalence has a specific condition. When energy distances use semimetrics of negative type, a corresponding kernel can be constructed so that the distance between distribution embeddings equals the energy distance exactly. The authors also characterize the probability distributions for which these induced kernels are characteristic, meaning that distinct distributions receive distinct embeddings.

The connection has practical consequences for choosing tests. The commonly used energy distance is one member of a parameterized family of kernels, and the authors show that other members can produce more powerful tests. This reframes a familiar statistic as one choice within a wider family. The result supports exploring those choices, while preserving the conditional nature of the equivalence and the possibility, rather than universality, of improved test power.
icml-2012-hypothesis-testing-using-pairw.tldr: The paper establishes a conditional equivalence between distance-based and kernel-based tests and identifies kernel choices that can improve test power.

paragraphs: The paper studies relational data arranged as a matrix, with subjects in rows and attributes in columns. Entries may contain either numerical or categorical values. Its goal is to uncover a compact hidden structure that describes both the subjects and the attributes while also representing correlations among them.

Each row and column receives a latent binary feature vector. A learned matrix maps a pair of these vectors to the corresponding observed entry. To model the binary features, the authors begin with multivariate Gaussian variables having low-rank covariance and transform them through a probit link. They apply this construction jointly to rows and columns.

The resulting Bayesian model infers low-dimensional binary descriptions alongside correlation structure among rows and among columns. Applications to real-world data demonstrate that it can recover meaningful compact structure from high-dimensional relational measurements. This matters because the representation describes both sides of the table and their relationships, giving a coordinated account of mixed data rather than treating each observed entry as an isolated quantity.
icml-2012-inferring-latent-structure-fro.tldr: A Bayesian model learns compact binary features and correlation structure for both rows and columns of mixed numerical and categorical data.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers a classifier from a labeled source domain to a target domain without target labels. The paper addresses this by learning the feature representation and classifier jointly. This links the search for shared features directly to the classification task they are meant to support.

The method seeks a feature space where source and target data have similar distributions while remaining discriminative. It optimizes an information-theoretic measure as a proxy for expected target classification error. Distribution alignment and class discrimination are therefore both objectives of the learned representation, with the proxy providing a way to pursue target performance without observing target labels.

The authors describe optimization using simple gradient-based methods and a way to cross-validate hyperparameters without labeled target examples. Experiments on visual object recognition and sentiment analysis support their modeling assumptions and show significant accuracy improvements over competing approaches. These findings provide empirical support for joint learning and the information-theoretic objective in the tested adaptation tasks.
icml-2012-information-theoretical-learni.tldr: Joint feature and classifier learning uses an information-theoretic objective to improve adaptation to unlabeled target domains in experiments.

paragraphs: Random projection changes the representation of data, raising a classification question: what happens to the margin separating classes? A useful representation should preserve the separation relevant to prediction. This paper examines that question directly by analyzing how a random projection can distort classification margins.

For binary classification, the authors give conditions under which the margin is preserved. This is a conditional result: using a random projection alone does not establish that class separation survives. The analysis identifies circumstances in which preservation can be supported theoretically, making the margin an explicit object of study when assessing the projected data.

The authors then extend their analysis to multiclass problems and derive theoretical bounds on margins after projection. This extends the question beyond separation between two classes to settings involving several possible labels. Together, the binary conditions and multiclass bounds provide a theoretical basis for reasoning about classification after random projection, with the central contribution being control of margin distortion rather than an unconditional preservation claim.
icml-2012-is-margin-preserved-after-rand.tldr: The paper gives conditions for preserving binary classification margins under random projection and theoretical bounds for multiclass margins.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether stochastic gradient descent is inherently slower than optimal methods for strongly convex stochastic optimization. A known guarantee for averaging its iterates was O(log(T)/T) after T steps, while another algorithm achieved the optimal O(1/T) rate. The authors investigate whether this gap reflects the algorithm or its analysis.

Their answer depends on smoothness. For smooth problems, stochastic gradient descent attains the optimal O(1/T) rate. For nonsmooth problems, however, averaging can genuinely incur an Ω(log(T)/T) rate. Thus, the extra logarithmic factor can reflect actual behavior rather than merely a loose mathematical bound.

The authors then show that modifying only the averaging step recovers the optimal O(1/T) rate. The underlying stochastic gradient updates need no other change. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The result makes the choice of returned estimate central: in this strongly convex setting, how iterates are combined can determine whether the method achieves the optimal rate, even when its update rule stays the same.
icml-2012-making-gradient-descent-optima.tldr: For strongly convex stochastic optimization, changing SGD's averaging step suffices to recover the optimal O(1/T) rate in the nonsmooth setting.

paragraphs: A changing network can contain neighborhoods with different patterns of evolution, such as communities that grow while others shrink. This paper proposes a nonparametric method for predicting links from a sequence of graph snapshots. It uses information about both candidate endpoints and the local neighborhoods around them.

Including neighborhood features allows the prediction model to account for different local dynamics within the same graph. The authors prove consistency of their estimator and provide a fast implementation based on locality-sensitive hashing. The work therefore addresses both the statistical behavior of the prediction method and the computational task of applying it efficiently.

Experiments use simulated networks and five real-world dynamic graphs. The method outperforms the state of the art in those evaluations, with particular gains when changes involve sharp fluctuations or nonlinear patterns. These findings support modeling local network context when forecasting links. They also connect the method's flexibility to the situations where the reported empirical advantage is especially pronounced.
icml-2012-nonparametric-link-prediction-.tldr: A consistent nonparametric link predictor uses endpoint and neighborhood features to model local dynamics, with strong results on fluctuating networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies function estimation when an underlying causal model can be identified. Its central question is how knowing the causal relationship should influence the choice of a learning approach. This makes causal knowledge part of deciding which information can help estimate a predictive function.

The authors discuss implications for covariate shift, concept drift, transfer learning, and semi-supervised learning. These scenarios raise questions about learning when distributions change or when different kinds of data are available. They argue that causal knowledge may support some approaches for a particular problem while ruling out others, so the suitability of a method can depend on the causal setting.

For semi-supervised learning, the paper formulates a hypothesis about when unlabeled data can help and presents empirical results that corroborate it. This is a hypothesis supported by experiments, rather than an unconditional promise that unlabeled examples improve prediction. The contribution is a causal perspective on selecting learning strategies, developed specifically for settings in which an underlying causal model is identifiable.
icml-2012-on-causal-and-anticausal-learn.tldr: The paper argues that identifiable causal structure can guide learning-method choices and offers an empirically supported hypothesis about when semi-supervised learning helps.

paragraphs: Coactive Learning models an interaction in which a system and its user share the goal of producing useful results. The system receives a context, such as a query, and proposes an object, such as a ranking. The user can respond with an improvement that need not be the best possible answer.

This feedback model allows learning from partial corrections instead of requiring an optimal target at every step. The authors argue that such improvements can be inferred from observable behavior, including search clicks. Their algorithms evaluate performance in terms of the user's numerical utility even though those utility values are never directly observed by the learner.

The proposed efficient algorithms achieve O(1/sqrt(T)) average regret. This gives a quantitative statement about how average regret decreases with interaction under the learning model. Demonstrations on movie recommendation and web search ranking show its applicability. The contribution links a relatively modest feedback requirement—an improved result—to learning guarantees and practical tasks involving structured outputs.
icml-2012-online-structured-prediction-v.tldr: Coactive Learning learns from user-provided improvements without observing utility values and achieves O(1/sqrt(T)) average regret.

paragraphs: A ranking system that assigns each item a fixed score for a query fixes the relative order of any two items. Yet consumer preferences can depend on which alternatives are shown: introducing a third item may change the preference between the first two. The paper develops a ranking model that can represent this behavior.

The Random Shopper Model represents each feature as a Markov chain over the items being ranked. Learning determines how much weight to give each feature so that the combined model reflects its importance. This provides a framework in which the set of available alternatives can influence the resulting ranking.

The authors show that the model can be learned through empirical risk minimization and give an efficient learning algorithm. On commerce search logs, their algorithm outperforms scoring-based methods, including regression and listwise ranking. These results support accounting for the alternatives presented to a shopper when predicting preferences, and demonstrate the empirical usefulness of the proposed model in commerce search.
icml-2012-predicting-consumer-behavior-i.tldr: The Random Shopper Model captures preferences that depend on available alternatives and outperforms scoring-based ranking methods on commerce search logs.

paragraphs: The paper gives a common mathematical interpretation of existing inference algorithms for latent Dirichlet allocation. It uses alpha-divergence projection as the organizing framework. This shifts attention to the divergence-based operations underlying inference, allowing algorithms to be understood through a shared description of how they form approximations.

Its main focus is CVB0, the version of collapsed variational Bayes inference that uses zero-order information. The authors explain this method through local alpha-divergence projections. The local perspective matters because it reveals the distinct projection operations that together make up the inference procedure.

Specifically, the paper shows that CVB0 combines projections with alpha equal to 1 and alpha equal to -1. Its interpretation therefore involves two choices within the divergence family. This result clarifies the mathematical composition of an existing method and contributes to the broader unification of LDA inference algorithms. The stated advance is an explanation of algorithmic structure, giving a precise way to relate CVB0 to the divergence framework.
icml-2012-rethinking-collapsed-variation.tldr: An alpha-divergence framework explains CVB0 inference for LDA as a combination of local projections with alpha values 1 and -1.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent approaches optimization by updating selected coordinates of a solution. This paper presents a general framework for parallel coordinate descent in large ℓ1 regularization problems. Its contribution includes a common formulation that accommodates both familiar sequential algorithms and methods designed to perform updates in parallel.

Cyclic coordinate descent and stochastic coordinate descent appear as special cases of the framework, as does the parallel Shotgun algorithm. Bringing these methods under one formulation connects different ways of organizing coordinate updates. The framework therefore provides a shared setting for describing established algorithms alongside additional parallel variants.

The authors introduce two such variants, Thread-Greedy coordinate descent and Coloring-Based coordinate descent, and report performance measurements from an OpenMP implementation. The work combines algorithmic unification with concrete implementations of new parallel methods. Its stated findings establish the breadth of the framework and provide implementation measurements; the abstract does not identify one method as uniformly fastest. The practical emphasis is on expanding the available ways to organize parallel coordinate descent.
icml-2012-scaling-up-coordinate-descent-.tldr: A general parallel coordinate descent framework includes existing algorithms and introduces Thread-Greedy and Coloring-Based variants with OpenMP performance measurements.

paragraphs: Some ranking tasks place particular importance on the items at the top of a list. This paper combines that objective with embedded feature selection, so learning the ranking function also determines which variables it uses. The aim is to obtain effective top-of-list rankings with a sparse scoring function.

The authors formulate the task as regularized empirical risk minimization using the infinite-push loss, corresponding to p equal to infinity, and sparsity-inducing regularizers. They address the resulting optimization problem with an alternating direction method of multipliers. This algorithm relies on proximal operators for the loss and regularizer, and the main technical contribution is a numerical scheme for the infinite-push loss's proximal operator.

Experiments on toy data, DNA microarray problems, and brain-computer interface problems show favorable comparisons with competing methods for ranking at the top while using fewer variables. The findings support learning ranking quality and feature selection together. The optimization contribution supplies the computational machinery needed to combine the specialized ranking loss with sparse models.
icml-2012-sparse-support-vector-infinite.tldr: Sparse infinite-push ranking combines top-of-list performance with feature selection through an optimization method built around a new proximal computation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to construct loss functions for prediction among multiple classes. It considers composite losses with two parts: a proper loss defined over probability distributions and an inverse link function. This representation separates the assessment of predicted probabilities from the transformation used to express a prediction as probabilities.

The authors establish conditions for convexity and strong convexity of these composite losses and explore their consequences. The distinction matters because propriety and convexity concern different aspects of a loss. The analysis examines how the probability-based loss and the inverse link combine to produce the curvature properties of the resulting objective.

The same separation also supports loss design. The authors show how to construct families of losses sharing the same Bayes risk, the best achievable expected loss for a given underlying distribution. This means the composite representation provides room to vary the loss while preserving that statistical quantity. The contribution is a theoretical framework connecting the components of multiclass losses to their convexity and to controlled choices in their design.
icml-2012-the-convexity-and-design-of-co.tldr: The paper establishes convexity conditions for composite multiclass losses and shows how to design loss families with the same Bayes risk.

paragraphs: Multiple observations of a network can help reveal recurring groups, but inconsistent edge sets make exact cliques difficult to identify. This paper introduces the most persistent soft-clique: a high-weight group of vertices that remains densely connected in all or almost all observed graphs, allowing some connections to be missing.

The method measures how close a vertex subset is to a clique by essentially counting the edges needed to complete it. Using that measure, the authors express the search in two ways: a max-min two-person game and a min-min soft-margin optimization problem. Both formulations yield the same solution when solved through a partial Lagrangian method.

Experiments on synthetic graphs and real social network data show reliable recovery of soft cliques despite random noise or unreliable observations. The approach makes persistence across observations part of the search objective while relaxing the demand for perfect connectivity. Its empirical findings suggest that this combination can recover meaningful recurring groups when individual graph observations disagree about some of their edges.
icml-2012-the-most-persistent-soft-cliqu.tldr: The paper finds high-weight, densely connected groups that persist across noisy graph observations using two related optimization formulations.

paragraphs: An f-divergence measures a discrepancy between probability distributions. Variational representations express such quantities through optimization and can serve as foundations for estimation methods. This paper shows that representations used in the literature can be tightened by restricting attention to probability measures, with implications for methods built on those representations.

The authors turn the tighter representation into a general estimator of f-divergence using two samples whose observations are independent and identically distributed. They also derive the estimator's dual optimization program. This connects the theoretical representation to a concrete estimation problem and provides an alternative optimization formulation for computing the estimate.

The dual program performs well empirically, and the authors identify a connection between their estimator and maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD. The contribution thus links a refinement in the representation of distributional discrepancy to a usable estimator and a relationship with another discrepancy measure. The reported empirical result supports the proposed estimation approach, while the tighter representation is the central theoretical advance.
icml-2012-tighter-variational-representa.tldr: A tighter variational representation of f-divergences yields a sample-based estimator, an empirically effective dual program, and a connection to MMD.
